lesson.title: sein, Motion & the Idiomatic Mindset
lesson.subtitle: ist↔is, war↔was — and Wie geht's = 'How goes it?'

hook.title: The Oldest Words Are the Closest
hook.content: ich bin ↔ I am? No — bin ↔ be/am both descend from the ancient *bʰu- 'to grow/be'; ich bin is 'I be' in the oldest sense. ist ↔ is: identical. war ↔ was: identical, one letter apart. The verb 'to be' is the most conservative word in any language — and German kept all three ancient roots: the *es- (ist), the *bʰu- (bin), the *wes- (war/gewesen). English kept the same trio: is, be, was. Then the idioms: Wie geht's? is literally 'How goes it?' — English used to say exactly that. Mir ist kalt is 'it is cold TO ME' — the dative feeling-grammar. German's idioms are frozen Early Modern English.

footnotes.title: Three Roots, One Verb
footnotes.content: Infinitive sein is a fourth root (*es- via 'sind'); the paradigm mixes *es- (ist, sind), *bʰu- (bin, bist), and *wes- (war, gewesen) — and English's is, are, be, was, was, been is the same mixed deck. Suppletion at the very core of both languages.

pattern.title: Being Cognates and the Idiom Fridge
pattern.content: The paradigm, with twins: ich bin ↔ I am/I be, du bist ↔ thou art, er ist ↔ he is, wir sind ↔ we are? (sind and are are different branches — but both ancient), er war ↔ he was (identical!), gewesen ↔ been. The idioms, unfrozen: Wie geht's? = 'How goes it?' (Es geht mir gut — 'it goes to-me well'). Es tut mir leid = 'it does me sorrow' (tun ↔ do!). Mir ist kalt = 'it is cold to-me'. Auf Wiedersehen = 'until re-seeing'. Each idiom is an English sentence your language used to say, wearing modern German clothes. Say them as whole gestures — that is how Germans store them too.
pattern.linguist_note: Es tut mir leid hides the do-tun twin: tun ↔ do is one of the oldest identical pairs in the language (Proto-Germanic *dōną). English built its do-support out of the same verb German uses for 'to do' — the auxiliary you learned NOT to use in questions is, historically, tun.

exercises.prompt: The being twins — match each form with its English cognate:
exercises.target_answer: ist, war, gewesen, bin, ich bin krank, ich bin satt, ich bin glücklich, ich habe Hunger
exercises.meaning: is, was, been, am, I am sick, I am full, I am happy, I am hungry
exercises.explanation: Three ancient roots (*es-, *wes-, *bʰu-) shared by both languages — the paradigm is a fossil bed, and the feelings ride it: krank, satt, glücklich, Hunger.

exercises.prompt: Unfreeze the idiom: 'Wie geht's?' literally asks what?
exercises.explanation: gehen + the dative: geht ES DIR? — 'does it go TO YOU?' English said 'How goes it?' until recently — and im Urlaub (on vacation), am Meer (at the sea), it still opens every conversation. holen fits too: sich Luft holen — to fetch fresh air — und holt sie wieder, fetches it again.

exercises.prompt: 'Mir ist kalt.' — what is happening grammatically?
options: The dative experiencer: it is cold TO ME
Mir is a typo for mich
exercises.target_answer: The dative experiencer: it is cold TO ME
exercises.meaning: Mir ist kalt — the methinks construction
exercises.explanation: Feelings happen TO you in German: mir ist kalt/langweilig/schlecht — the dative of experience.

exercises.prompt: 'Es tut mir leid' hides which common English verb in 'tut'?
exercises.meaning: tun ↔ do (it does me sorrow = I am sorry)
exercises.explanation: tun and do are the same ancient verb — Es tut mir leid is 'it does me sorrow'. The polite apology is an English sentence in disguise.

exercises.idea: you're summing up the weekend: yesterday was good and today you're cold — the German way, it is cold to me
cues: war ↔ was opens the first clause; the second is the dative experiencer: heute ist mir kalt — 'it is cold TO ME'
exercises.target_answer: Gestern war gut und heute ist mir kalt
exercises.meaning: Yesterday was good and today I am cold (it is cold to me)
exercises.explanation: war ↔ was in the first clause, the dative experiencer (mir ist kalt) in the second — the being verbs and the idiom fridge in one sentence.

summary.outcome: Conjugate sein via its English twins and use the frozen-English idioms.

use_example.german: Gestern war gut, aber heute ist mir kalt.
use_example.english: Yesterday was good, but today I am cold.

summary.takeaway: ist↔is, war↔was, bin↔be — and the idioms are unfrozen English: How goes it? It does me sorrow. It is cold to me.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: ist, war & bin — the being cognates: the sein paradigm through its English twins.

twist.prompt: Your friend caught the chill: today I am cold (it is cold to ME) becomes it is cold to HIM.
twist.explanation: mir → ihm: the dative experiencer has three faces, all English fossils — 'give it me', 'give it thee', 'give it him'. The idiom needs the TO-case: ihm, never ihn.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

hunger.context_translation: I have great hunger / I am very hungry.

krank.context_phrase: Ich bin krank und bleibe zu Hause.
krank.context_translation: I am sick and staying home.
krank.etymology_derivation: Old sense 'crooked, weak' — Wiktionary: cognate with English crank. [wiktionary]

satt.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sat, Proto-Germanic *sadaz, meaning sated or full; the exact cognate is English sad, which originally meant sated before it drifted to its modern sorrowful sense. [wiktionary]

glücklich.etymology_derivation: Glück (luck) + -lich; Wiktionary: 'Compare English luck' — a relative via Dutch. [wiktionary]

urlaub.context_phrase: Ich fahre im Urlaub nach Italien.
urlaub.context_translation: I go to Italy on vacation.
urlaub.etymology_derivation: Middle High German urloup 'permission to be away', kin to erlauben — cognate with English leave. [wiktionary]

meer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. English mere is the listed cognate, and Latin mare is cognate through Indo-European. [wiktionary]

holen.context_phrase: Ich hole Wasser aus der Küche.
holen.context_translation: I am getting water from the kitchen.
holen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *holōną (to fetch); the page documents cognate English haul — the same hauling-and-fetching word. [wiktionary]

wieder.context_translation: We will see each other again.
wieder.etymology_derivation: Old High German widar 'against', from West Germanic *wiþr 'toward, against' — the page names English wither and widdershins as cognates; German wieder turned against into again. [wiktionary]

toilette.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French toilette around 1700 — the very same French word that English took as toilet. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
